explanations.explanation: Army is right, baker. God says He will "…bring you out with all your army…" and then lists horses, horsemen in full armor, shields, bucklers and swords. That's a whole lot of gear for one prince. I can barely get my cookie boxes stacked straight.

Gold does show up in this passage, but later. In verse 13, Sheba, Dedan and the merchants of Tarshish ask Gog whether he has come "…to make off with silver and gold…" In verse 4, what comes out with him is his army. So gold isn't what God says He will bring him out with.

This passage doesn't mention Gog's gods at all. Verse 4 says God will bring him out with all his army. Then it lists horses, horsemen in full armor and a great company with shields and bucklers. That list is soldiers and gear.

True. God says, "Get ready; prepare yourself, you and all your company gathered around you…" It's a call to get set, and it takes in the whole company, not just Gog. Me, I get ready by hunting for my apron, and I've never needed a company for that.

This one is true, so False isn't what the text says. God tells Gog, "Get ready; prepare yourself, you and all your company gathered around you…" That means Gog and the company around him, together. Easy to miss when so many nations are on the guest list.

That's the one. God says the land has people "…gathered from many nations to the mountains of Israel, which had long been desolate." So a place that sat empty for a long time has people living in it again. Sounds like a bakery that finally got its lights back on.

The text never says that. Gog hasn't even arrived yet when the land is described, since God says he will enter it in the latter years. The people already living there are ones gathered from many nations. Gog is coming to them, not leaving soldiers behind.

Sheba and Dedan do show up in this passage, but verse 8 doesn't name them as the ones on the mountains of Israel. In verse 13, they and the merchants of Tarshish ask a question about loot. The people verse 8 names are the ones gathered from many nations.

The text doesn't say that. God describes the people of that land as ones who "…all now dwell securely." Gog also calls them "…a quiet people who dwell securely…" Fear isn't the word either of them uses.

False is right, baker. God says the people were brought out from the nations and "…all now dwell securely." They're settled and at ease. That calm is what Gog will later point to when he makes his plan.

Yes, an evil plan. God says, "On that day, thoughts will arise in your mind, and you will devise an evil plan." The thoughts show up first, and then the scheme takes shape. I've had thoughts show up in my head too, but mine were mostly about extra chocolate chips.
No treaty here. God says Gog will devise "…an evil plan." And what follows in his own words is about going up against a quiet people. Nothing in there is about making peace.
Merchants do come up in this passage, but Gog's plan isn't a trade deal. God says he will devise an evil plan. The merchants of Tarshish and the others only ask him about loot later in verse 13.

explanations.answer: They live without walls or gates
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Gog says he will come against "…a land of unwalled villages…" and a quiet people, "…all of them living without walls or bars or gates…" Those are his own words about the people he plans to attack. I think he sees a place with no defenses and starts counting the plunder.

explanations.answer: Their land still lies in ruins
explanations.explanation: Not quite. The land had long been desolate, but God says it has recovered from war and Gog describes "…desolate places now inhabited…" So the places that were empty have people in them again. Gog's focus is on how the people live, with no walls, bars or gates.

The text says the opposite. Gog talks about "…a people gathered from the nations, who have acquired livestock and possessions…" Those are people living there, with animals and belongings. Empty villages wouldn't be worth the trip, and that's not what he says.
True. Gog says he will go "…in order to seize the spoil and carry off the plunder…" Those words are part of the plan God says he will say in verse 12. He says it plainly, about the quiet land.

This one's true. Gog says he is going "…in order to seize the spoil and carry off the plunder…" Those are his own words in the plan. So False isn't what the text says. He's after what the quiet people have.

The text points the other way. God says, "…you will come from your place out of the far north…" Beth-togarmah is also named earlier as coming from the far north. South doesn't show up in the direction at all.
False is right, baker. God says Gog will come "…from your place out of the far north…" with many peoples. They're all riding horses. The direction God gives is north, not south.

explanations.answer: So the nations may know Him
explanations.explanation: That's the reason God gives. He says, "…so that the nations may know Me when I show Myself holy in you before their eyes." It's about the nations seeing who He is. Gog is coming, but God is the one in charge of the whole thing.

explanations.answer: So Gog's own people are punished
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't give that reason. The reason God states is "…so that the nations may know Me when I show Myself holy in you before their eyes." It's about the nations knowing Him. Punishment of Gog's own people isn't the purpose named here.

explanations.answer: So Israel's army can be tested
explanations.explanation: The text never says this. Israel's army isn't mentioned in this passage at all. God says He brings Gog "…so that the nations may know Me when I show Myself holy in you before their eyes." The reason is about the nations knowing Him.

Prophets, yes. God asks if Gog is the one "…of whom I have spoken in former days through My servants, the prophets of Israel…" So God's question points back to what He spoke in former days through the prophets. The text says they prophesied for years in those times.

Kings don't appear in that verse. God says He spoke through "…My servants, the prophets of Israel…" The ones who prophesied for years are the prophets. A king may have a crown, but a prophet is the one with the message here.

Priests aren't named here. God says He spoke "…through My servants, the prophets of Israel, who in those times prophesied for years…" So the word came through prophets. It's a small word swap, but the text is clear.

True. God says, "Now on that day when Gog comes against the land of Israel, declares the Lord GOD, My wrath will flare up." It's a heavy line, so I'll say it plainly. The timing is the point: it's on the very day Gog comes against the land.

This one's true. God says, "Now on that day when Gog comes against the land of Israel, declares the Lord GOD, My wrath will flare up." So False isn't what the text says. It's a heavy line, and it comes right from God.

That's right. God says the fish of the sea, the birds of the air, the beasts of the field, every creature that crawls on the ground and "…all mankind on the face of the earth will tremble at My presence." That's the sea, the sky and the ground all in one list. Nothing in that list is left out.

The sun and moon aren't in the list. God names the fish of the sea, the birds of the air, the beasts of the field, every creature that crawls upon the ground, and all mankind. Those are the ones who "…will tremble at My presence."

Angels aren't listed here. The ones God names are the fish, the birds, the beasts, every crawling creature and all mankind on the face of the earth. They "…will tremble at My presence." This list is about creatures here on earth.

The text says the opposite. God says, "The mountains will be thrown down, the cliffs will collapse, and every wall will fall to the ground." The verse says every wall, not just some of them. Mountains and cliffs come down too.

False is right, baker. God says the mountains will be thrown down, the cliffs will collapse, and "…every wall will fall to the ground." That's mountains, cliffs and walls, all coming down. It's a heavy picture of how big this earthquake is.

That's right. God says, "And I will summon a sword against Gog on all My mountains, declares the Lord GOD, and every man’s sword will be against his brother." It's a heavy line. The swords are turned on brothers.

The beasts of the field show up in the earthquake verse, where they tremble. But in verse 21 God says "…every man’s sword will be against his brother." So the swords are turned on brothers, not animals. It's a different verse and a different picture.

The merchants of Tarshish show up back in verse 13, where they ask their question. In verse 21 God says, "…every man’s sword will be against his brother." So the verse names a brother, not the merchants, as what each sword is against.

explanations.answer: His troops and the nations with him
explanations.explanation: Yes. God says He will pour out torrents of rain, hailstones, fire and sulfur "…on him and on his troops and on the many nations with him." So it falls on Gog and everyone who came along. This is a heavy part, and God is the one doing it.

The text doesn't say that. God says the torrents of rain, hailstones, fire and sulfur fall "…on him and on his troops and on the many nations with him." That's Gog and the ones who came with him. The people living in the land aren't named there.

Nineveh isn't in this passage. It's the city God told the prophet Jonah to go to (Jonah 1:2; 2 Kings 14:25). Here God says the torrents of rain, hailstones, fire and sulfur fall "…on him and on his troops and on the many nations with him." That means Gog and the ones who came with him.
